# Account of the Prediction Record — where and why we were wrong

**Owner:** M5 (Muhammad Muhaimin bin Abdul Rahman) · written 9 Oct 2026, after all measurements.
**Inputs:** `docs/prediction_record.md` (frozen 7 Oct, before the first benchmark), `docs/prediction_outcomes.md` (generated by `tools/compare_predictions.py`), `results/requirements_check.md`, and the raw evidence cited per section.

The prediction record is not edited. This file explains each WRONG verdict: what we assumed, what the logs show, and which part of our mental model was off. Two of the twenty scored claims were right (accuracy rises with size; no model meets R4), and so was the bottleneck prediction (§5).

---

## 1. Single-request latency: every model about 2× slower than predicted

| Model | Predicted p50 | Measured p50 | Ratio | Predicted size factor (vs 1B) | Measured size factor |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| qwen2.5:0.5b | 1.2 s | 2.5 s | 2.1× | ×0.4 | ×0.43 |
| llama3.2:1b | 3.0 s | 5.7 s | 1.9× | ×1 | ×1 |
| llama3.2:3b | 8.1 s | 16.2 s | 2.0× | ×2.7 | ×2.85 |
| qwen2.5:7b | 18.0 s | 34.1 s | 1.9× | ×6 | ×6.0 |

Source: `results/accuracy/summary_*.json` (`latency_ms.p50`), sequential harness, golden set.

**What was right:** the *shape*. Scaling the 1B figure by parameter count predicted the size factors almost exactly (last two columns). Prefill share was 95–98 % of Ollama time for every model, as predicted (≥ 70 %).

**What was wrong:** the *base*. Every prediction was scaled from one 1B calibration (`results/logs/prefreeze_calibration_pc.jsonl`, 17 probes, 7 Oct 21:55 SGT) whose prefill rate was **110 tok/s**. Every later 1B measurement on the same machine ran at about half that:

| 1B run | Prefill rate (median) |
|---|---|
| Calibration probes, 7 Oct | 110 tok/s |
| Load test, 1/min, 8 Oct 02:11 SGT | 56 tok/s |
| Accuracy run, 8 Oct 09:15 SGT | 52 tok/s |

Source: `ollama_prompt_eval_ms` and `prompt_eval_count` in `results/logs/requests.jsonl`. The golden prompts are not longer than the probes (median 277 vs 334 tokens), so prompt length does not explain it. During the accuracy run Ollama was pinned at ~395 % CPU (`results/logs/dockerstats_accuracy_llama3.2_1b.txt`), so it was compute-bound. We did not record CPU or the runner configuration during the calibration, so we cannot say whether the probes ran under different conditions (thread/quota setting, a warm shared-prefix cache, or host state).

**Why our mental model was off:** we treated one 2-minute calibration as a stable property of the machine and scaled four models from it. A rate measured once, by a different harness, before the test configuration was final, is a single run, and the brief's own rule applies: a single run is not a measurement. We should have calibrated with the same harness and settings as the test and repeated it.

## 2. Accuracy: the small models failed in a way we did not anticipate

| Model | Predicted | Measured (95 % CI) | Most frequent answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| qwen2.5:0.5b | 45 % | 12.0 % (8–18 %) | "6" (Consumer loan) on 143 of 175 tickets |
| llama3.2:1b | 58 % | 22.3 % (17–29 %) | "7" (Money transfer) on 119; "1" (Credit reporting) on 56 |
| llama3.2:3b | 70 % | 44.6 % (37–52 %) | "5" (Bank account) on 95 |
| qwen2.5:7b | 82 % | 73.1 % (66–79 %) | spread across all seven (13–38 each) |

Source: `results/accuracy/summary_*.json` (confusion matrices) and `raw_completion` in `results/logs/requests.jsonl`.

**What we assumed:** small models would read the narrative and get the *fine distinctions* wrong, for example latching onto "credit report" in a debt-collection complaint (record §2).

**What happened:** the 0.5B and 1B models mostly did not classify at all. They returned nearly the same list number for every ticket. The 1B model's answers sit almost entirely on the first and last items of the numbered list. The 3B model leans heavily on item 5. The prompt asks for "the category number and nothing else" (`service/app/classifier.py`, prompt v1). We chose the numbered format *because* we expected it to help small models; for these two models it gave them a cheap answer that ignores the text. Only the 7B model's errors look like the semantic confusions we predicted.

**Why our mental model was off:** we modelled accuracy as a smooth function of size and treated the prompt as neutral. Below a size threshold the output format dominated. The ordering prediction survived (RIGHT), but the gaps did not. Changing the prompt is optimisation and belongs to Assignment 2; the baseline is reported as measured.

The **unparsed-rate** predictions (8 % for 0.5B, 3 % for 1B) were also wrong, in the opposite direction: 0 % for every model. The same behaviour explains it: a single digit always parses.

## 3. Hardest and easiest categories, and the largest confusion

`compare_predictions.py` scores these on recall averaged over the four models: hardest **Credit card** (23 %), easiest **Consumer loan** (55 %). Both are WRONG against our Debt collection / Mortgage prediction. The average is dominated by the collapsed small models from §2: 0.5B's 86 % Consumer-loan recall comes from answering Consumer loan for almost everything.

Looking only at qwen2.5:7b, the one model that classifies normally:
- **Easiest = Mortgage (91 %)**, as predicted.
- **Hardest = Money transfer or service (46 %)**, which we ranked 2nd hardest. Debt collection, our predicted hardest, reached 85 %.
- **Largest confusion = Money transfer → Bank account (11 of 26)**, the reverse of our predicted pair (Debt collection → Credit reporting: 1 ticket). The 3B model shows the same pair at a larger scale (22 of 26).

**Why our mental model was off:** we expected the debt-on-credit-report overlap to be the hard case because it dominated *our* labelling disagreements. The models resolved it far better than the transfer-vs-account boundary, where a P2P or wire complaint describes money leaving a checking account. Our ranking also assumed every model would rank categories the same way (record §3); the collapsed models make that ranking meaningless below 7B.

## 4. Stress limit and capacity: 7.4 tickets/min predicted, about 2/min measured

| Ladder | Max sustainable | Completed at the 2/min step | Saturated throughput | Errors |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | none (backlog at 2/min) | 1.0/min | 1.80/min | 54 |
| 2 | none (backlog at 2/min) | 1.2/min | 1.68/min | 56 |
| 3 | 2/min (4 still in flight; just within the rule) | 1.2/min | 4.05/min | 0 |

Source: `results/stress/stress_llama3.2_3b_run*.summary.json`, `results/stress/run_stress.log`.

**Two separate errors.**

1. **Inherited latency error.** We derived 7.4/min as 60 s ÷ 8.1 s (predicted 3B single latency). At the measured 16.2 s the same formula gives 3.7/min, so half of the miss is §1.
2. **The single-server model was wrong.** We assumed requests queue one after another, each taking S seconds. Ollama actually ran 4 parallel slots (`--parallel 4`) on 10 threads inside a 4-CPU quota (`results/stress/ollama_log_stress_llama3.2_3b.txt`, runner command line). Concurrent requests share the CPU and each one slows down. The load tests show this already at the 1/min peak: 3B p95 was 79 s against a 32 s single-request p95.

**Failure mode: we predicted latency growth with no errors, because we believed the timeout was 600 s.** The service's backend timeout is **300 s** (`OLLAMA_TIMEOUT_S`, `service/app/config.py`). In ladders 1–2, 110 requests reached it and returned 502. Ollama logged "aborting completion request due to client closing the connection" for them, so CPU already spent on those requests produced nothing. That is why saturated throughput fell to 1.7–1.8/min in ladders 1–2 but reached 4.05/min in ladder 3, where no request reached 300 s.

**Why our mental model was off:** we checked the config file we remembered rather than the one that ran, and we treated Ollama's parallel slots as adding "no throughput" without asking what they do to *latency* under overlap.

## 5. What we got right: the bottleneck

All of the record's §1 bottleneck predictions held, and none of its "would prove us wrong" observations occurred:
- Ollama CPU at ~395 % (its full 4-CPU quota) under load; the triage service under 6 % (`results/logs/dockerstats_load_*.txt`).
- Prefill 94–99 % of Ollama time per request (record: ≥ 70 %).
- Service latency matched Ollama's own time to within 0.1 s, so the queue sits inside Ollama, not in the service.
- `GET /search` p95 stayed at 33–61 ms in every run (record: falsified above 1 s).

## 6. Requirements we expected to fail (record §4) vs the requirements check

| Claim in record §4 | Outcome | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| R4: no candidate meets it; 7B closest at ~82 % | none meets it; 7B closest at 73.1 % | RIGHT (the figure was 9 points high) |
| R5: 7B narrowly passes | 7B fails: Money transfer 46 %, Credit card 58 %, Consumer loan 64 % | WRONG |
| R6 unparsed fails for 0.5B | 0 % unparsed for every model | WRONG (see §2) |
| R1 fails for 3B and 7B, from single latency not queueing | fails for 3B and 7B, but mainly from queueing and contention (3B p95 79 s vs 32 s single) | half right |
| R2 and R3 met by all four | R2 met by all; R3 fails for 3B (87 % of offered completed) and 7B (22 %) | WRONG for R3 |

Source: `results/requirements_check.md`.
